Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> In Focus | National Government steps up efforts to tackle open defecation and improve sanitation Source : Myjoyonline.com 18 November 2026 5:25pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs says it is pursuing measures to strengthen sanitation management and address persistent challenges, particularly open defecation.
The Ministry’s Technical Advisor for Sanitation and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), Michael Forson, said government was working with partners to improve waste management systems and encourage private sector investment in converting waste into renewable energy.
He was speaking at the opening of this year’s World Toilet Day commemoration, where he represented the Deputy Minister.
Mr Forson said the Ministry would support such investments through policy alignment, regulation and collaboration with private investors and development partners.
“The ministry will work with partners to make sure more private sector are engaged in turning our waste into renewable energy and others. First, we will align policy so that approaches like this one are recognized and supported in our national plans.
“Second, we will give practical backing through clear regulation and help with land where it is needed. Third, we will work with private investors and development partners so that more communities benefit from such investment,” he said.
He stressed that ending open defecation would require collective action beyond government institutions and local authorities.
“No ministry can end open defecation alone, nor can any assembly end it alone. It will be ended in homes, in schools, in markets, and in places of worship if we all work together,” he added.
The Member of Parliament for Ashaiman, Ernest Henry Norgbey, also called for stronger collaboration among government, municipal assemblies and residents to improve sanitation.
He said local authorities could provide infrastructure and develop policies, but their efforts would have limited impact without public cooperation.
“Government and the Assembly may provide the necessary infrastructure and policies, but without the cooperation of the people, our efforts will not achieve the desired results,” he said.
Mr Norgbey urged residents to take responsibility for keeping their communities clean and supporting efforts to eliminate open defecation.
“I urge all residents to support the assembly's effort to eliminate open defecation by ensuring that every household has access to and use of decent toilet facilities,” he said.
Beyond access to toilets, the safe collection, treatment and disposal of human waste remain central to addressing Ghana’s sanitation challenges.
The Managing Director of Safisana Ghana Ltd, a company that converts faecal sludge into renewable energy, said waste recycling could help reduce environmental pollution while creating useful resources.
He warned that rapid urban growth was placing pressure on existing sanitation infrastructure, particularly sewer networks in Accra and surrounding communities.
“We live in a city and not just a Ashaiman, but also Accra that grows faster than its sewer networks. And this puts public health at risk. It pollutes the environment and it takes away the people's dignity who are not able to just go to a clean toilet,” he said.
Ghana will mark World Toilet Day on November 19 under the theme, “Safe toilets. Equal futures.” The observance highlights the links between access to safe sanitation and gender equality.
